h1: Health claims on functional and alcohol-free drinks in India
title: Health Claims on Alcohol-Free Drinks | Craft Beer School
desc: What Indian drinks brands can and cannot say about health on functional and alcohol-free drinks. Learn how to write claims safely.
teaser: Gut friendly, immunity, detox. Each of those words on a label is a claim. Claims need more than good intentions.
standfirst: Functional and alcohol-free drinks sell on how they make people feel. That is exactly where brands get into trouble. This guide explains how claims are treated in India and how to write copy that is honest, useful and less likely to be pulled.
sections: Every word on the can is a claim

A brand builder sees a label as a place to tell a story. A regulator sees every word and image on it, on your website and in social posts as a claim about the product. Words like immunity booster, detox, gut healing or good for digestion are health claims. A picture of a beating heart or a doctor in a white coat can be treated the same way.

In India, food and non-alcoholic drinks are regulated by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI). Its Advertising and Claims Regulations set out how claims on food are made and substantiated. The rules and their interpretation are updated over time, so read the current text or ask a food regulatory consultant before you finalise anything. Nothing here is legal advice.

It helps to sort claims into a few kinds, because each is treated differently.

  • Nutrition claims describe what is in the drink, such as low sugar, no added sugar or source of vitamin C. These usually have defined thresholds that the product must meet.
  • Health claims link the drink or an ingredient to a body function, such as supporting digestion. These need scientific substantiation. Some kinds need approval.
  • Disease claims say a product treats, cures or prevents a disease. Foods and drinks cannot make these. That territory belongs to medicines.

Words like natural, fresh, pure and traditional also have rules about when they can be used. Check them before you build a brand name around one.
Where kombucha and functional drinks get caught

Kombucha is often sold as gut friendly or probiotic. A live kombucha does contain microbes, but that does not mean it delivers a proven benefit at the dose in a bottle. Probiotic claims in particular are tightly controlled. The evidence needed is specific to the strain and the amount. Our guide to kombucha and water kefir production explains why live cultures are hard to keep consistent, which makes any benefit claim harder still.

Drinks with added ashwagandha, turmeric, ginseng or other herbs face a second set of questions. Some of these ingredients are covered by specific standards or permitted lists for nutraceutical or health supplement categories, with limits on dose and wording. A herb being traditional in Ayurveda does not by itself make it permitted in a carbonated drink at any level.
Alcoholic drinks cannot make health claims

If your drink contains alcohol above the limit for a non-alcoholic drink, the rules tighten again. FSSAI's standards for alcoholic beverages do not allow health claims on them. Nutrition claims are restricted too. Alcohol advertising is also restricted in India, which our guide on alcohol advertising rules in India explains.

That matters for brands that sell both. An alcohol-free version of a beer brand cannot be used to carry health messaging back to the alcoholic product. Keep the claims, artwork and social copy for each product separate.

Here is a working method for brand teams:

  1. List every claim, word and image across the label, website, social media and sales decks.
  2. Sort each into nutrition, health or disease. Strike out anything that sounds like a disease claim.
  3. For each nutrition claim, check the threshold and prove it with a lab analysis of the finished drink, not the recipe.
  4. For each health claim, ask what evidence you hold and whether the claim and the dose match the regulation.
  5. Get a food regulatory consultant to review the final list before printing.

Then describe what the drink is and how it tastes. Brewed with green tea and ginger. Lightly sparkling. 25 calories a can, if the lab says so. Facts like these are safe and they often sell better than vague promises.
The brand story without the risk

You do not need health claims to build a strong alcohol-free brand. People choose these drinks to skip alcohol for an evening, to drive home, to keep up with friends or simply because they like the taste. A brand that speaks to those moments, with real flavour and an honest label, earns trust that lasts longer than a buzzword.

Craft, provenance and process are fair game. Where the ginger is grown, how long the tea brews, why the drink is unpasteurised and what that means for storage are all claims you can stand behind. They also give your social media something real to talk about.

A claim that breaks the rules can lead to a notice, a demand to change labels, withdrawn stock or penalties. Reprinting costs money too. It can also attract complaints from competitors or consumer groups. Treat label review as part of product development, done before the first print run, rather than a last minute check.

Keep a file for each product with the lab reports, ingredient specifications and the reasoning behind every claim. If a question ever arrives, that file is your answer.
faqs: Can I call my kombucha probiotic in India?
Probiotic claims are tightly controlled and need strain-specific evidence at the dose delivered. Get a food regulatory consultant to review any such claim first.
It can be treated as one. It is also hard to substantiate. Most brands are safer describing ingredients and taste instead.
Can an alcoholic drink carry health claims?
No. FSSAI's standards for alcoholic beverages do not allow health claims on them. Nutrition claims are restricted too.
What claims are usually safe to make?
Factual descriptions such as ingredients, flavour and process, plus nutrition claims that meet the defined thresholds and are backed by a lab analysis of the finished drink.
